entries.what_happened: Two manuscripts claim a negative answer, each by exhibiting a group with an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton over a finite field. (1) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two': for a finite field K of characteristic two, a finitely presented group G containing an element of odd prime order, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1 (Theorem 1.1). The coefficients of b give a local rule with memory supp(b). The map Tᵦ: K^G→K^G on all configurations is injective, because a is a left inverse, and not surjective, because a point indicator δₕ with (ba−1)ₕ≠0 has no preimage. Its corollary on non-surjunctivity states that G is not surjunctive. Its F∞ corollary also gives an overgroup U with the same failure, conditional on an external embedding theorem. (2) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic': for p the least prime divisor of (m!)²+1 with m = binom(1200,600), an odd prime, a field K of order p⁴, a finitely generated group G with torsion, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1. Its Section 06 applies the same transfer to these sums, giving an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton on K^G, and states that this negatively answers Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture. 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite' and 'A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture' do not treat cellular automata.
entries.delivers: If the claims hold, they answer the list's question negatively. The question asks whether every group is surjunctive, for every finite alphabet, with every injective cellular automaton surjective. One group, one finite alphabet and one injective non-surjective automaton refute that, and each of (1) and (2) supplies one. Restrictions: each gives a single group. In (1) the alphabet is a finite field of characteristic two whose order the text does not state, and the group is finitely presented with odd-order torsion. In (2) the alphabet has order p⁴ for the one prime p above, and the group is finitely generated with torsion. The manuscripts' statement matches the list's: they define surjunctive as every injective cellular automaton over every finite alphabet being surjective, and they state Gottschalk's conjecture as 'every group is surjunctive'.
entries.remains: Nothing in the list's question, if the claims hold. The question is a universal yes/no over all groups and names no subclass, and the manuscripts make no claim about the surjunctivity of other specific groups.
entries.object: The cellular automaton Tᵦ on all configurations K^G, with local rule given by the coefficients of b and memory set supp(b), together with the group G and its sums a, b. None is written out. In (1) the sums come from a terminating finite prescription that the text says has not been executed. In (2) G and K are built from finite formulas and a specified prime, with no computed instance.
entries.conditional_on: (1) Termination of the finite search for the incidence data uses Linnik's theorem, via a uniform bound cited from Xylouris, and the paper's own hypergraph existence theorem. The non-surjunctivity of its overgroup U depends on an external companion embedding theorem; the claim for G itself does not. (2) No unproven hypothesis is stated. The construction draws on published constructions for some ingredients (Haviv; Golovnev and Haviv; Dykema and Juschenko), but the text says it proves the matrix and group steps itself.
entries.doubts: (1) The authors say the prescription 'has not been executed', and that no practical execution of the finite search is asserted. The witnesses are established by termination proofs and algebraic certificates rather than by a computed instance. (2) The text says the construction 'is not claimed to have been evaluated as a practical computation' and concerns only the one prime p. It does not evaluate p.

entries.what_happened: Four manuscripts claim a nonsofic group, all by the same route: Elek and Szabó's theorem that group algebras over fields are stably finite for sofic groups would make the group algebra directly finite, contradicting the scalar defect. (1) 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite': its finitely presented torsion-free group G over F₂ is said, in the introduction, to be not sofic, by Elek–Szabó Corollary 4.7. (2) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two': its finitely presented group G with odd-order torsion is nonsofic (abstract and introduction). Its F∞ corollary also calls an overgroup U nonsofic, by the same route applied to U. (3) 'A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture': its finitely generated group G_D = (⊕ over H₂ of C₃) ⋊ H₂, with H₂ taken from the characteristic-two paper's scalar pair, is said to be not sofic. The argument applies Elek–Szabó's determinant bound for sofic groups to the positive integral matrix A*A. The paper calls this an external consequence, not used to build A. (4) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic': its finitely generated group G with torsion is said, in the introduction only and not the abstract, to be nonsofic by Elek–Szabó's theorem.
entries.delivers: If the claims hold, each refutes the universal statement, since one discrete countable nonsofic group suffices, and each manuscript gives one. Restrictions: (1) torsion-free, finitely presented, over F₂, with a finite two-dimensional classifying complex. (2) finitely presented, characteristic two, with odd-order torsion; the text asserts finite presentation in a section I did not check. (3) finitely generated, with the determinant-bound obstruction. (4) finitely generated, with torsion, over a field of order p⁴. On the statement: (2) uses Elek–Szabó's finite-map definition. For every finite E in the group and every ε in (0,1), there is a finite Ω and a map σ from the group to the self-maps of Ω that is approximately multiplicative on E, nearly the identity at 1, and moves almost every point for g in E∖{1}. This matches the list's approximate-multiplicativity and almost-free conditions. The list speaks of maps into permutations, whereas this uses all self-maps of Ω, and the text does not argue that the two versions agree.
entries.remains: Nothing for the universal yes/no question, if the claims hold. The list names no subclass, and the manuscripts claim no positive result about soficity of any other group.
entries.object: In each case the nonsofic group itself: (1) a finitely presented torsion-free group built from cones on finite labeled graphs drawn from a random model; (2) a finitely presented group G with odd-order torsion, and its overgroup U of type F∞; (3) G_D; (4) a finitely generated group with torsion. None is written out. Each is given by a finite prescription or a probabilistic existence argument, and the characteristic-two prescription is stated to be unexecuted.
entries.conditional_on: All four rely on a cited published theorem that the manuscripts do not prove: Elek–Szabó (2004, Corollary 4.7) for (1), (2) and (4), and Elek–Szabó (2005, Theorem 5, the determinant bound for sofic groups) for (3). (2)'s overgroup U also depends on an external companion embedding theorem. (3) takes its existence input from the characteristic-two paper's scalar pair, a separate manuscript in this family.
entries.doubts: (2) Its nonsoficity is only as firm as its scalar pair, which the text says has not been executed as a computation. (3) The text itself calls the sofic conclusion 'an external consequence, not an ingredient in constructing A'. (4) The nonsoficity claim appears only in the introduction, and the abstract omits it.
